body:
Just FYI, this PR largely seems to be a duplicate of (and would thus supersede) #101064 and #101083, except those happen at the physics server level instead.

I suppose this approach is preferrable over those ones, since it would apply to all physics servers.

I might be wrong but from user land I don't see anything else in the api that requires keeping track of objects other than `self` and cleaning them up before you're allowed to free `self`, which is a bit of a trap. I think the ideal solution is for it to be handled automatically by engine code. But ultimately the question is _where_ should we clean up these exceptions from freed bodies?

1. In `get_collision_exceptions` as this PR currently stands
2. In the deconstructor of `GodotBody2D`, perhaps aided by a new `PhysicsServer2D::remove_all_collision_exceptions_with(body)` method
3. in the collision detection code where the exceptions are actually used (not sure where this)
4. leave it as the user's responsibility but improve the error messaging and docs
5. some other option I haven't thought of

If we go with option 1 I'd probably go with #101083 over this PR as it is more thorough and prevents even the first error message from being shown.

I don't like option 2 as it would require iterating through every body in the simulation and searching its exceptions for the one we want to remove. The exceptions are a `VSet` which helps but it is the "iterating over every body" part I am scared of. Perhaps if we cached a lookup of these at the server level, or maybe a cached reference in the _other_ body that is part of the exception at the time we add it?

I presume option 3 wouldn't work at all as the wouldn't ever be a collision with a freed object to test against?

> If we go with option 1 I'd probably go with #101083 over this PR as it is more thorough and prevents even the first error message from being shown.

The fact that collision exceptions are implemented as just a proxy for the physics server methods is somewhat problematic to begin with, since any physics server getter (e.g. `body_get_collision_exceptions` and `body_get_object_instance_id`) will force synchronization with the physics thread when running with the `physics/*d/run_on_separate_thread` setting enabled, so if you call `get_collision_exceptions` from `_process`, or the "wrong" signal callback, you will inadvertently shoot yourself in the foot from a performance standpoint.

I feel like `PhysicsBody3D` might be better served by actually storing the list of exceptions itself, in the form of something like `LocalVector<ObjectID>`, much like how we cache a bunch of other things "redundantly" in the physics nodes already to prevent synchronization with the physics server.

With that approach, we could at the very least do all this at the scene node level, rather than force every physics server to care about it, which I don't think should need to care about this.

This would mean that the current `body_get_object_instance_id(body_rid)` call and subsequent `instance_id.is_null()` check would be replaced with an `ObjectDB::get_instance` lookup instead, and you could do something based on whether that resulting `Object` casts to a `PhysicsBody3D` successfully or not.

What that "something" should be, I'm not sure. I do still think that having a getter do garbage collection on the list it's returning is a bit of a code smell, but at the same time, just emitting a warning/error that there are stale references in the list won't do the user much good, since they can't really remove the stale exceptions without a valid `Node` reference anyway, which they likely won't have if the exception is truly stale.

---

I guess one idea (that builds upon the `LocalVector<ObjectID>` stuff above) is to recognize the fact that collision exceptions are always a two-way thing. You only need one of the two bodies to have an exception for the other in order for the collision to be ignored, so body `A` having an exception with body `B`, but body `B` not having an exception with body `A` serves no functional purpose.

This means that we could simply make it so that when body `A` adds a collision exception with body `B`, you also add an exception in body `B` with body `A`. That way you still end up with the exact same behavior, but the list of collision exceptions actually reflects all the bodies that you won't be colliding with. Then you simply iterate over that list during `NOTIFICATION_EXIT_WORLD` (or maybe `NOTIFICATION_PRE_DELETE`) and let the other bodies know that you're going away, so that they can remove that reference from their list as well.

That way you also don't end up with what can be seen as a "memory leak" just because you never call `get_collision_exceptions`.
Doesn't seem to be a clear way forward and other PRs cover the same ground, so closing this.
